title: Krishna Carries Off Rukmini
story:
Krishna loved a woman, and she was about to be given to another man. Rukmini was the princess of Vidarbha, daughter of Bhishmaka, the king of Kundina, and her beauty was spoken of across the kingdoms. Krishna had asked for her hand, but her brother Rukmin, who hated him, refused the match. Then, at the urging of Jarasandha — the powerful king who had long been Krishna's enemy — her father promised her to Shishupala, king of Chedi. Between a powerful father and a proud brother her future was settled. The wedding drew near, and kings from across the earth gathered in Kundina for it, Shishupala's allies among them: an armed ring of princes come to see the princess given away.

Krishna, too, had come to Kundina, with Balarama, his elder brother, and many of the Yadus, his own people, at his side. The city was full of banners and of soldiers, for half the kings of the earth had arrived, and the roads were thick with their chariots and elephants.

On the day of the ceremony Rukmini went to the temple to pray, as a bride does before she is given. The temple stood at the edge of the city, and the princess went up its steps alone while the noise of the gathered kings gathered like a storm behind her and the whole court waited outside the doors. When she came out and stepped toward her chariot, the assembled princes fell silent. She was radiant; the sight of her struck the waiting kings still on their elephants, their horses, and their chariots, and some slipped from their seats in their daze. She pushed a strand of hair back with her left hand and glanced shyly over the gathered princes — and her eyes found Krishna, waiting in the crowd. For a long moment no one moved, as though the whole assembly understood at once what was about to happen.

Before anyone could move, Krishna swept her up. He set her on his own chariot, the one that flew the banner of Garuda, the great eagle, and drove through the ring of kings as a lion drives through a pack of jackals, carrying off the share that was his. The princess made no move to stop him. All the banners, the ceremony, the armed guests — all came to nothing in the space of a single breath.

The proud kings could not bear it. Jarasandha and the rest stood shamed, their honor torn away, and cried aloud that their fame, won with their bows, had been snatched from them by cowherds — like a lion's kill stolen away by deer. They surged after the chariot, and Rukmin himself swore he would never set foot in Kundina again until he had slain Krishna. But Balarama and the Yadus turned and met the pursuers, threw them back, and held the road while Krishna rode on.

When Rukmin overtook the chariot alone, Krishna scattered his army as if in sport and flung him to the ground, and would have ended him then and there. But Rukmini begged for her brother's life. "He is my only brother," she said. "Do not kill him. Give him to me." And Krishna spared Rukmin at the entreaty of the woman he had just carried off. Rukmin kept his vow and never returned to Kundina; he founded a city of his own, Bhojakata, and dwelt there ever after.

And Krishna married Rukmini in due form, having won her openly, before the eyes of the very kings who had meant to give her to another. In time she bore him a son, Pradyumna, whom the old accounts call a portion of the god of love come back to the world.
reflection: The episode is often called an abduction, but what Krishna does is openly claim a bride in front of the very kings who had gathered to give her to another. There is no concealment in it; the drama is that every armed prince in the assembly watches it happen and none of them can stop it.
tradition_note: The Bhagavata places the carrying-off at Rukmini's svayamvara, as she came out from the temple; the Vishnu Purana sets it on the eve of her betrothal to Sisupala and adds the pursuit and defeat of her brother Rukmin. This telling follows the Bhagavata for the abduction and draws the closing detail of Rukmin's defeat from the Vishnu Purana.
hero_scene: Krishna, driving a chariot flying the banner of Garuda, sweeps Rukmini up from beside her own chariot and turns to ride through a ring of stunned, falling kings as the princess looks back over her shoulder.
visual_elements: a chariot with the Garuda banner
a ring of kings on elephants, horses and chariots
